summary: MPLS and GMPLS networks can be built from layered networks, and efficient end-to-end paths need to span layers. This document extends PCEP so path computation requests and responses can handle multiple layers, including how to ask for a path that crosses them.

eli5.summary: Think of a trip that uses a highway and a ferry. The route planner has to plan across both kinds of travel, not just one.

questions: how does pcep support multi-layer paths
what is the pcep inter-layer object
what do pcep metric types 18 and 19 mean
subtitle: New PCEP objects and metrics that let a path computation request span several network layers.

tldr.problem: MPLS and GMPLS networks can be built from layers, and a router in a higher layer may not know the lower-layer topology, so it cannot compute an end-to-end path across layers by itself.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds four PCEP objects (INTER-LAYER, SWITCH-LAYER, REQ-ADAP-CAP, SERVER-INDICATION) and two metric types, so a client can say whether inter-layer paths are allowed and a PCE can report what kind of path it computed.
tldr.outcome: It satisfies the requirements in RFC 6457 and is a Proposed Standard with no obsoleting or updating RFC listed.

today: RFC 8282 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2017. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
A Path Computation Element (PCE) computes a network path from a network graph and constraints. A Path Computation Client (PCC) asks it for paths using the PCE Communication Protocol, PCEP. A PCE can also initiate or modify services by supplying new paths.

A network may have several layers, for example packet switch capable (PSC), time division multiplex (TDM) and lambda switch capable (LSC) layers. Label Switched Paths (LSPs) in lower layers carry higher-layer LSPs. The topology formed by lower-layer LSPs, advertised as traffic engineering (TE) links in the higher layer, is called a Virtual Network Topology (VNT).

The RFC argues that resources should be optimized across all layers rather than layer by layer. That is inter-layer traffic engineering. This document gives PCEP the extensions needed for it, satisfying the requirements in RFC 6457.
sections.eli5: Some networks are stacked like floors in a building. This RFC teaches the route planner to plan a trip that uses more than one floor.

sections.title: PCE-Based Inter-Layer Path Computation
sections.content:
A router in the higher layer might not have information about the lower-layer topology, particularly in an overlay or augmented model, so it may not be able to compute an end-to-end path across layers. Using PCEs solves this in one of two ways.

  • A single PCE holds topology information for several layers and computes the whole path.
  • Several cooperating PCEs each know one or more layers, but not all, and collaborate on the end-to-end path.

A hybrid node may advertise a single TE link with multiple switching capabilities. Such links normally sit at a layer or region border, so a PCE must be able to give server-layer path information when the PCC needs it. RFC 5623 describes the models in more detail, including the Virtual Network Topology Manager (VNTM).
sections.eli5: Either one planner knows every floor, or several planners each know a few floors and talk to each other to plan the whole trip.

sections.title: The INTER-LAYER Object
sections.content:
The optional INTER-LAYER object (Object-Class 36, Object-Type 1) can appear in PCReq and PCRep messages, and also in PCRpt, PCUpd and PCInitiate messages. Its body is 32 bits: reserved bits and three flags. In a request, if the object is absent, the PCE MUST act as though inter-layer computation were disallowed (I flag zero).

  • I flag: in a request, whether an inter-layer path is allowed. In a reply, whether the returned path is an inter-layer path. If I is clear, a returned path MUST NOT be an inter-layer path.
  • M flag: in a request, whether a multi-layer path (set) or a mono-layer path (clear) is wanted. In a reply, which kind was returned. It is ignored when I is clear.
  • T flag: in a request, whether triggered signaling is allowed. In a reply, whether it is required to support the returned path. It is ignored when I is clear.

If I is set, M is clear and T is clear, virtual TE links that have not been pre-signaled MUST NOT be used, and loose hops spanning the lower layer MUST NOT be specified, which is equivalent to I being clear. Reserved bits MUST be sent as zero and SHOULD be ignored on receipt.
sections.eli5: The object is a little card with three yes/no boxes: may we use more than one floor, do we want a path that really spans floors, and may new connections be built on the fly.

sections.title: The Other Objects and Metrics
sections.content:
Three more optional objects and two metric types complete the extensions.

The SWITCH-LAYER object (class 37) lists switching types and encoding types, each with an I flag. When the flag is set, the computed path MUST traverse a layer with that combination. When it is clear, the path MUST NOT enter or traverse such a layer. Combinations not listed MAY be traversed. It is only valid alongside an INTER-LAYER object; without one, the PCE treats inter-layer computation as disallowed.

The REQ-ADAP-CAP object (class 38) asks for an adaptation capability at both ends of a lower-layer LSP, using a Switching Capability and an Encoding field. It is used when the PCE for higher-layer paths acts as a PCC toward a PCE for lower-layer paths.

The SERVER-INDICATION object (class 39) in a reply marks the path in the Explicit Route Object (ERO) as server-layer information and describes that layer's switching capability and encoding, with optional TLVs.

The new metric types are 18, "Number of adaptations on a path", and 19, "Number of layers on a path". A request using either MUST have the PCE minimize or bound that quantity.
sections.eli5: Extra cards let you say which kinds of floors you must or must not use, what kind of connector you need between floors, and whether the route shown is for the lower floor. Two new scores count how many connectors and floors the trip uses.

sections.title: Request, Reply and Stateful Procedures
sections.content:
A PCC requests or allows inter-layer computation by including the INTER-LAYER object with the I flag set in a PCReq. Multiple Objective Function (OF) objects MAY be present: the first applies to the higher layer and later ones to successive lower layers. When a PCReq or PCRep carries more than one request or path, an INTER-LAYER object is used per request or per path.

On success, the PCRep MAY include the INTER-LAYER object, and the I, M and T flags describe the path returned. The PCE MAY give server-layer path information in the ERO, in which case the reply carries at least two sets of ERO information, one for the client layer and one for the server layer, marked by SERVER-INDICATION. The PCC can then trigger signaling to set up the LSPs. On failure, the PCRep contains a NO-PATH object, and SWITCH-LAYER and/or REQ-ADAP-CAP MAY indicate which constraints could not be met.

For stateful PCEs (RFC 8231) and PCE-initiated LSPs (RFC 8281), the same objects and metrics are used on PCRpt, PCUpd and PCInitiate messages. Section 5 of the RFC updates the PCReq and PCRep message formats, in Routing Backus-Naur Form, to include the new objects.
sections.eli5: You ask for a trip and say whether you can use several floors. The planner answers with the route and says what kind of trip it is, or tells you which of your rules it could not meet.

sections.title: IANA Assignments
sections.content:
IANA assigned Object-Class values 36 (INTER-LAYER), 37 (SWITCH-LAYER), 38 (REQ-ADAP-CAP) and 39 (SERVER-INDICATION) in the PCEP Objects registry, and metric values 18 and 19 in the Metric Object T Field registry.

IANA also created the "Inter-Layer Object Path Property Bits" registry for the INTER-LAYER flags. New bits need "IETF Review". Bit 29 is T, bit 30 is M and bit 31 is I; bits 0 to 28 are unassigned.
sections.eli5: The official list of numbers got new entries for the new cards and scores, and a new list was started for the three yes/no boxes.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Inter-layer traffic engineering with a PCE may raise new security issues when PCE-to-PCE communication crosses layer networks. Issues may also arise when a single PCE has full visibility of TE information for several layers.

The Path-Key-based mechanism of RFC 5520 MAY be applied to protect topology confidentiality between layers.
sections.eli5: Sharing maps of every floor with a planner can reveal secrets, so the RFC points to a way to hide the details of one floor from another.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Sent as zero and ignored on receipt.

items.label: INTER-LAYER
items.desc: Whether inter-layer paths are allowed or returned.

items.label: SWITCH-LAYER
items.desc: Layers a path must or must not traverse.

items.desc: Requested adaptation capability at both ends of the lower-layer LSP.

items.label: SERVER-INDICATION
items.desc: Marks ERO path data as server-layer information.

items.desc: Number of adaptations on a path.

items.desc: Number of layers on a path.
